en: If a person should stand even for a single moment at the gateway of a temple,
he shall attain by that alone the fourfold liberation.
Śrī Hari should be sung of with the mouth, and Hari should be sung of with the mouth.
Who indeed could calculate that merit which is born from the remembrance of Hari?
It is always proclaimed in the Vedic scriptures with a great voice: "If even a creature dwelling in the cycle of existence hastens [to remember Him] with its tongue, it crosses over. 2-3.
Jñāneśvara says this:
because he observed the secret signs of Vyāsa, the Lord of Dvārakā has come in person to the house of the Pāṇḍavas.
He who is called Jñāna is celebrated in the four Vedas; he who is called Kāraṇa is celebrated in the six Śāstras; and Hari himself is sung of in the eighteen Purāṇas. 4–5.
Śrī Hari is to be grasped from the churning of the world like butter; abandon useless talk and abandon wandering on the wrong path.
(2) Hari and the Self are one and the same, pervading all, equal in the individual soul and in Śiva; do not vainly set your mind upon difficult and wrong paths.
(3) This Hari is the form of Vaikuṇṭha, as recited by Jñānadeva; Śrī Hari is seen everywhere, woven like warp and woof throughout all things. (4)

That which possesses the three qualities (*triguṇa*) would be devoid of essence, whereas that which is essence itself is without qualities (*nirguṇa*). This investigation into the essential and the non-essential is now considered in the recitation of Hari’s names. (1) Whether with qualities or without qualities, it is traditionally known as such through its connection to qualities; yet, if the mind is attached there without Hari, it is useless.
(2) For this Śrī Hari is unmanifest and likewise formless; since from Him alone the moving and unmoving world was born, worship that very Śrī Hari. (3)
The remembrance of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in meditation occurs within the mind of Jñānadeva; in this way, merit is accumulated by men through infinite births.
Devotion devoid of feeling, liberation without devotion, and the capacity for action without strength—such talk is in vain. 1–2.
"How might the favor of the gods be swiftly granted to me?"—this for which you strive again and again is in vain; remain motionless.
Though you strive and strive repeatedly throughout this phenomenal world day and night, [it is all to no avail].
Relying upon what objective support do you not worship Śrī Hari?
Jñānadeva says that the recitation of Śrī Hari’s name must be performed;
by that alone, through such firm resolve, there shall be the subduing of phenomenal existence.
There is no accomplishment through the practice of yoga, nor even through the ritual of sacrifice;
these dharmas are merely forms of hypocrisy and are nothing but useless pretenses.
There is no God without devotion, nor is there the destruction of doubt.
Direct experience does not exist without a true guru.
(2) The Lord is not for one who lacks austerity, nor are riches for one who does not give.
Who indeed would speak what is beneficial without a conversation of love in solitude? (3)
Jñānadeva speaks: no example is effective here;
the means for crossing over is obtained only through association with the virtuous.
He who has been awakened by the virtuous should remain free from egoism.
Through direct experience, that state of equal flavor (samarasa) arises within the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
and just as the light of camphor increases in its own place,
once ignited, it reaches its completion right there in that very same place.
Liberation itself has come to the feet of the devotee of Hari;
by good fortune, the devotee is adorned and likewise becomes a servant of the holy ones.
In the mind of Jñānadeva, there arose a longing for the company of the virtuous.
In the forest of worldly existence, through that very [realization] of the self-essence, there is the vision of Hari.
Likewise, those who are not devotees commit sins as massive as mountains;
those sins become as firm as adamantine cement.
Those who have no devotion for Hari are undevoted and fallen;
because they do not worship Hari, they are considered ill-fated.
Though eloquent, they vainly spread a web of words.
Even though Śrī Hari is compassionate, he is not attained by these worlds.
According to the view of Jñānadeva, the Self, the means of knowledge, and likewise wealth—all these reside as one complete being within the heart of everyone. 3–4.
The dissolution of the mind is attained through association with the virtuous;
therefore, the Lord of Śrī is certainly to be reached by this very path.
The expression "Rāma-Kṛṣṇa" is remembered as the state of the individual soul (jīvabhāva).
This chanting of the name of Rāma is indeed renowned as the very self of Śiva. The name of Hari, whose essence is the one reality, is said to be the means of accomplishment;
and for those who accomplish it, the bond of duality does not obstruct them.
The devotees of Viṣṇu possess a supreme relish for tasting the nectar of the Name;
it is that very science of long life which has been mastered by the yogis. The firmness in the chanting of the Name was already present in Prahlāda even during his childhood.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself gave instruction to Uddhava:
"The Lord of Knowledge says that the practice of chanting the Name is considered easy;
for only a rare few understand how difficult other spiritual practices are. (5-6)
If one’s mind is not fully devoted to Rāma or Kṛṣṇa,
his recitation of the *apaviṣṇu* mantra is in vain, and that knowledge is likewise useless.
He who, though born, does not know the path of non-duality (*advaita*), is truly unfortunate.
How could his entry into Rāma or Kṛṣṇa possibly occur?
(2) How indeed could the chanting of the names of Hari be possible for those by whom the knowledge that destroys duality was not obtained from their guru? (3)
Jñāneśvara says that which is called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna) is that by the recitation of whose names this phenomenal world attains peace;
or it is simply wandering at the confluence of the three rivers and at various sacred pilgrimage sites.
If the mind is not engaged in the chanting of the Name, all that wandering is in vain.
He who is averse to the Name is indeed embodied sin;
no one is able to uplift such a sinner except for Hari.
Vālmīki, renowned in the Purāṇas, has said this:
"One may uplift the three worlds by remembering the name of Hari.
Jñānadeva declares this: whoever should chant the name of Śrī Hari.
His entire ancestral lineage becomes purified.
By the utterance of Hari’s names, infinite heaps of sins all go to complete destruction in a mere moment,
just as grass becomes like fire through contact with fire.
In that same way, the sin of one who chants the name of Śrī Hari perishes.
This utterance "Hari" is a mantra endowed with power;
out of fear of this mantra, even the afflictions caused by malevolent spirits flee.
Jñānadeva says: Śrī Hari is capable for me, yet He is likewise inaccessible even to all the Upaniṣads;
there is no perfection through holy places, vows, or observances when they are devoid of devotion.
Alas, O people! This form, which is empty of reality and a mere vain adjunct, is clearly perceived by you as if it were an amalaka fruit held in the palm of your hand;
yet Hari is known through the power of true being (bhāva), and not otherwise.
Just as a drop of mercury situated on the ground cannot be grasped even with hundreds of efforts,
so too Hari cannot be grasped even with hundreds of means.
Jñāneśvara says that cessation is the qualityless Guru.
He bestowed upon my two hands the full state of abiding in one's own true nature.
It must be understood that concentration on Hari is not possible without the bliss of the equality of Brahman and the self;
concentration is not achieved through a dualistic intellect. 1.4–5.

Without samādhi, no further glory of the Buddha exists; by Keśava alone are all perfections attained. Whether it be supernatural power, accomplishment, or a treasure-trove, such attributes are merely vain.
As long as the mind is not fixed upon Śrī Hari, that supreme bliss,
so Jñānadeva says: "Through constant meditation on Hari,
that delightful state of meditative absorption (samādhi) has been attained by me."
Whoever should daily perform the recitation of Hari’s names mentally with a fixed number,
for him there shall be no affliction, even as measured by time.
The chanting of the names of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa is considered equal to an infinite mass of austerity.
By him, multitudes of sins are reduced to ashes.
O Śaṅkara, he who mutters this mantra— "Hare, Hare, Hare"—
and those others who mutter this mantra, they too attain liberation.
Jñāneśvara says this very thing: "By the recitation of the name of the Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa, I attained my own supreme abode;
there is oneness with that name, and duality with any other name. (4)
A rare person indeed knows the non-duality of Hari and his name.
Through recitation with an even mind, equanimity toward Hari is realized;
and from the remembrance of Śrī Hari comes the perfection of tranquility and self-control.
Just as the thousand-rayed sun is the illuminator of all things, so does Rāma alone shine forth among both the moving and the unmoving.
The Lord of Knowledge says in my heart: "May there be constant remembrance of Hari."
By that, my liberation from future births has been secured.
Reciting "Rāma, Kṛṣṇa" is very easy for human beings;
nevertheless, a man who chants the name of Hari is rare in this world.
By those men who have accomplished the dissolution of the mind within the names "Rāma" and "Kṛṣṇa," all perfections (siddhis) whatsoever have been attained. Perfection,
wisdom, and likewise righteousness— these are the followers of Hari.
Even while remaining in the world of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one may attain the dissolution of the mind through association with the virtuous.
Jñāneśvara says to me: "The mudrās 'Rāma' and 'Kṛṣṇa' reside within my heart;
by that alone, the ten directions have become the very nature of my Self."
If a person sings the glory of the recitation of Hari with his mouth,
his body certainly becomes purified;
the great merit that comes from austerity is then concentrated within his limbs.
He lives for many millions of kalpas and rejoices because of that.
His mother, father, brother, and many kinsmen—
all these stand before him as forms of Viṣṇu, four-armed.
"That knowledge which is both hidden and attainable—its cessation is now within my grasp;
he has granted it, and thus it has been obtained by me," so spoke Jñāneśa.
"The Harivaṃśa, the Purāṇas, and the chanting of Hari’s name."
For that man to whom no object whatsoever is pleasing except for Hari,
it is his great gain that he should attain Vaikuṇṭha;
he shall also obtain the fruit of all pilgrimage to sacred sites.
He who has traveled by the path of the mind does not attain this happiness;
but that man who is steadfast in the recitation of Hari becomes blessed.
Jñāneśvara says: "In my association with the Name, there is true flavor."
My devotion has always been directed toward Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
The single essence of all spiritual practices is the constant chanting of Nārāyaṇa;
in this matter, the authority consists of the Vedas as well as the words of the Upaniṣads.
It should be understood that chanting, austerity, ritual action, religious observance, or even dharma—
all this is in vain without the Name.
Bees that have taken refuge in a flower-kalika remain with their minds attached to it alone.
Likewise, those who take refuge in the recitation of Hari have their minds attached to Hara.
The word of the Lord of Knowledge is a scripture of name-mantras that bestows power;
for one who bears His name, both lineage and family are freed from Yama.
The chanting of the names of Viṣṇu is remembered as the means for devotees;
within them, it destroys endless and infinite sins.
Through penance performed over countless births, the single name of Śrī Hari alone is equal [to all else].
The recitation of Hari’s names is easily accessible on all paths.
Yoga, sacrifice, ritual action, dharma, and likewise adharma—all this is merely illusory; it dissolves within the recitation of Hari.
Jñāneśvara says: Sacrifice, yoga, dharma, and likewise ritual action—all of this is the form of Hari; there is no other rule for me.
There is no restriction whatsoever regarding the utterance of His name or any formal observance.
In this matter, there is the deliverance of both the speaker and the listener alike.
This name "Rāma-Kṛṣṇa" is remembered as the remover of all defects;
for both sentient beings and insentient things, Hari alone is the savior.
By the utterance of Hari’s name, this tongue becomes possessed of its true purpose;
who indeed is capable of describing the good fortune of one who merely bears His name?
Jñāneśvara says that the recitation of Hari, along with all its ancillaries, is [the goal] by its very nature.
Those who first bear the name go to Vaikuṇṭha without effort;
those people who constantly and regularly remember the Name are rare to find,
for that Beloved of Lakṣmī is always present near them.
Those men who always chant the name "Nārāyaṇa,
Hari," in their homes there is always enjoyment as well as the fourfold liberation.
Know that a birth without the name of Hari is like a life in hell.
Such a living being will certainly become a guest in the world of Yama.
When Jñāneśa asked about the greatness of the Name, Nivṛtti said: "The Name is more pervasive even than the sky. 3-4.
Seven, five, three, and ten—when these are all combined together, this entire collection shines within Hari, who is of the nature of the single reality.
This is indeed not so; for that [reality] is the most excellent among all paths.
Not even the slightest difficulty is experienced in the remembrance of the Name.
(2) That very "I am the Swan" within the vital breath is known as the ajapā-japa;
and in that japa as well, the remembrance of the Name is certainly present. (3)
Jñāneśvara says that life devoid of the Name is useless;
therefore, I am following this path called Rāma-Kṛṣṇa.
Recitation, austerity, ritual action, duty, restraint, or even religious merit—[all these are in vain].
"Rāma is everywhere"—this is the cause for generating pure devotion.
O friend, you must not abandon this disposition; rather, doubt alone must be abandoned.
Let the proclamation of the names of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa be made at all times.
Even if you possess birth, wealth, lineage, character, and noble ancestry in every way, nevertheless, being endowed with devotion, worship Śrī Hari with urgency.
3. The Lord of Knowledge tells me: "Mentally recite 'Rāma-Kṛṣṇa' during meditation."
Therefore, my residence is always in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Neither existence nor non-existence is found anywhere in Śrī Hari;
therefore, through the chanting of Hari’s name, the attainment of liberation shall always occur.
Wherever the utterance of the names "Nārāyaṇa" and "Hare" is found—
Neither the Kali age nor Time itself is worthy of entry there;
even the Vedas do not know the measure of His power,
so how could ordinary living beings understand it?
"Jñāneśvara has declared that the recitation of Hari is the very fruit [of practice];
by that, all lands became for me like Vaikuṇṭha itself.
O mind, hold fast to this one truth alone: His Name. (5)
Through that, a state of compassion for you, Hari, will arise.
O Rāma, utter those names—Suvāca, Kṛṣṇa, or Govinda—with a voice faltering;
chant that very name first.
There exists no reality higher than the Name, nor indeed any other;
therefore, your journey by any other path is useless.
The Lord of Knowledge, remaining silent while holding Śrī Hari within, speaks thus.
Having fashioned a garland of these names in my mind, I constantly recite them within my heart.
This is the conclusion of the six treatises: that the "tasting of all happiness" resides in the Name.
Therefore, do not be averse to the Name for even half a ghaṭikā. 4–5.
This entire worldly activity of saṃsāra is indeed false;
coming and going therein would be in vain without the name of Hari.
By the mere recitation of the mantra of His name, even ten million sins are destroyed.
Therefore, let your resolve be firm in the chanting of the names of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Conceal your own nature and shatter all illusion;
do not hide yourself from this tranquility and self-restraint by following the impulses of the senses.
Faith should be cultivated toward sacred sites and religious observances, as well as through tranquility, compassion, and mercy;
you must honor Hari as a guest.
That which is known by the Knower of Wisdom has been declared as the measure of knowledge by the one who has attained liberation.
That Saṃjīvana-samādhi is accomplished through the recitation of this [text] concerning Hari.
In this recitation of Hari, there are twenty-one verses;
they were composed by Jñāneśvara regarding the power of the names of Viśva. 1.6–7.
The man who constantly recites this on the banks of the Indrāyaṇī river will certainly and in every way attain supreme authority. Furthermore,
the practitioner should do so with a one-pointed mind and a tranquil heart.
One should likewise perform the remembrance of the Name with great joy even in the midst of [other] activities. At the final moment of life, as well as during times of distress—
whether externally or internally— Hari watches over them.
This has been experienced by many virtuous and noble persons;
how, then, could a man who is lazy and dull-witted cross over it?
Having heard these words, full of love, from the true guru Nivṛtti, [he was moved].
Every moment, Jñānadeva attained supreme contentment.
